d: A collection of writings published in honor of a scholar
ety: Borrowed from German Festschrift, from Fest (“celebration; festival”) + Schrift (“writing (work of an author)”).
s: Incandenza's burial in Québec's L'Islet County was twice delayed by annular hyperfloration cycles. Cornell University Press announced plans for a festschrift.

d: Given to merry frolicking
ety: From frolic + -some.
s: To some, the very word "playsuit", with its frolicsome associations, will induce the conviction that this is not an item of clothing to be seen alive in.

d: Of or associated with or requiring the use of the mind
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek νοητικός (noētikós), ultimately from νοέω (noéō, “I see, understand”).
s: Homeric Greeks valued clichés because not only the poets but the entire oral noetic world or thought world relied upon the formulaic constitution of thought.

d: Flow in an irregular current with a bubbling noise
ety: From Middle English burblen (“to bubble”), imitative.
s: She burbled on, as if I cared to listen.

d: Adroitness in using the hands
ety: From Middle English sleighte, sleyght, sleythe, from Old Norse slœgð (“cunning”), from Proto-Germanic *slōgiþō, from *slōgiz (“cunning”) (whence English sly). Doublet of sly and slöjd/sloyd.
s: If men have so many sleights to compass their matters, how can the compasser himself hold his fingers?

d: Flower arrangement consisting of a circular band of foliage or flowers for ornamental purposes
ety: From Middle English chapelet, from Old French chapelet. Doublet of chapelet.
s: People often pray the chaplet at 3:00 pm to commemorate Jesus' death.

d: Repetition of same sense in different words
ety: From pleonasm + -astic.
s: `a true fact' and `a free gift' are pleonastic expressions.

d: Pretentious or silly talk or writing
ety: An alteration of twattle (1556), of unknown origin.
s: You're talking a load of twaddle. Get your facts straight, man!

d: Kill one in every ten, as of mutineers in Roman armies
ety: The verb is first attested in 1591, the noun in 1641; borrowed from Latin decimātus, perfect passive participle of decimō (“to kill one tenth; to tithe”) (see, from -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (noun-forming suffix)), from decimus (“tenth”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix). As a noun, via Latin decimatus (“tithing area; tithing rights”).
s: Shall we decimate them? That sounds good, nice word. Remove one-tenth of the population!

d: Someone of remarkable excellence
ety: US origin, perhaps a blend of hummer (“something that moves fast”) + dinger (“something outstanding”). First attested in a newspaper article in the Daily Enterprise of June 4, 1883, at Livingston, Montana.
s: Most of the questions were pretty easy, but that last one was a humdinger.

d: Someone who attacks in search of booty
ety: From maraud + -er.
s: If she keeps the dog up, the garden is invaded night and day by an army of peregrinating feline marauders that scent the booty from afar.

d: The range of interest or activity that can be anticipated
ety: From Middle English purveu (“proviso”), from Anglo-Norman purveu est (“it is provided”), or purveu que (“provided that”) (statutory language), from Old French porveü (“provided”), past participle of porveoir (“to provide”), from Latin prōvideō (see provide). Influenced by view and its etymological antecedents.
s: Rhetorical relations have truth conditional effects that contribute to meaning but lie outside the purview of compositional semantics.

d: Armor carried on the arm to intercept blows
ety: From Middle English bukler, bokler, bokeler, bokeleer, from Old French bocler, boucler, bucler, (French bouclier) from Vulgar Latin *bucculārius (“bossed”), from Latin buccula (“boss”). Merged with buckle + -er.
s: I am eight times thrust through the doublet, four through the hose, my buckler cut through and through; my sword hacked like a hand-saw -- ecce signum!

d: The underside of a part of a building (such as an arch or overhang or beam etc.)
ety: From French soffite, from Italian soffitto, from Vulgar Latin *suffīctus, perfect passive participle of Latin suffīgō (“to fasten or fix onto”).
s: The elevation of the pipe soffit is 10.4 meters above mean sea level.

d: Sad beyond comforting; incapable of being consoled
ety: From Medieval Latin discōnsōlātus (“comfortless”), from dis- (“away”) + cōnsōlātus (“consoled”).
s: For weeks after the death of her cat she was disconsolate.

d: A laborer who loads and unloads vessels in a port
ety: From Spanish estibador (cognate with Portuguese estivador, and compare Medieval Latin stivator), from estivar, estibar (“to load”), from Medieval Latin stivare, stīpāre (compare Italian stivare, stipare), the present active infinitive of stīpō (“to cram, fill, stuff”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *steypos, which is from the root Proto-Indo-European *steyp-. It is cognate with stiff through Pr
s: The work of discharging and loading cargoes other than coal is undertaken by master stevedores, who are employed by the shipowner.

d: An elderly man
ety: From gaff (“hook”) + -er. * (cinema): The natural lighting on early film sets was adjusted by opening and closing flaps in the tent cloths, called gaff cloths or gaff flaps. * (glass)
s: And you're here to tell me what's what. Just like your bloody gaffer promised.

d: A mistake in printed matter resulting from mechanical failures of some kind
ety: Borrowed from Latin errātum, neuter of errātus (“mistaken”).
s: When the journal's editors found out about the misreported details, they issued an erratum.

d: Sharply contrasted in character or purpose
ety: From Latin antitheticus + -al.
s: His wrong-headed beliefs are antithetical to everything we stand for as a community.

d: Container for coal; shaped to permit pouring the coal onto the fire
ety: From Middle English scuttel, scutel, from Old English scutel (“dish, platter”), from Latin scutella, diminutive form of Latin scutra (“flat tray, dish”), perhaps related to Latin scutum (“shield”); compare Dutch schotel and German Schüssel.
s: She scarce gave me time to return her salute, before she quitted the shop with an easy scuttle, and stepped again into her coach

d: A mayor or chief magistrate of a Spanish town
ety: Borrowed from Spanish alcalde, from Arabic اَلْقَاضِي (al-qāḍī, “the judge”). Doublet of qadi and casis.
s: There's to be a fair, you know. The alcalde announced it. He's got a good head for business, our alcalde has.

d: Found in the ordinary course of events
ety: Middle English werkedei, from Old Norse virkr dagr (“working day”). Cognate to later workday; see work and day. Used in adjective sense from 16th century. By surface analysis, work + -a- + day. First attested in c. 1200.
s: But then something started to shift—the Burning Man aesthetic was creeping into the workaday world; festival culture went mainstream.

d: A formal or authoritative address that advises or exhorts
ety: From Latin allocūtiō (“address”).
s: The Minister of War, in a barrack-square allocution to the officers of the artillery regiment he had been inspecting, had declared the national honour sold to foreigners.

d: A despicable coward
ety: From Middle English dastard (“a dullard”), most likely formed from *dast, a base derived from Old Norse dæstr (“exhausted, breathless”) + -ard. Compare Icelandic dasaður (“exhausted”), dialectal Swedish däst (“weary”), Middle Dutch dasaert, daasaardt (“a fool”), English dazed (“stupefied”).
s: I thought ye would never have given out these arms till you had recovered your ancient freedom: but you are all recreants and dastards, and delight to live in slavery to the nobility.

d: A method of athletic training (especially for runners) in which strenuous effort and normal effort alternate in a continuous exercise
ety: Borrowed from Swedish fartlek, from fart (“speed”) + lek (“child’s play”).
s: Interval workouts are typically more intense and structured than strides and fartleks. If you have access to a track, distance is easier to gauge.

d: A monument built to honor people whose remains are interred elsewhere or whose remains cannot be recovered
ety: From French cénotaphe, from Ancient Greek κενός (kenós, “empty”) + τάφος (táphos, “tomb”). By surface analysis ceno- + -taph.
s: A cenotaph was erected for him in Gaul, while his body was taken to Rome and inclosed in a magnificent tomb.

d: Steadiness of mind under stress
ety: From French équanimité, from Latin aequanimitās (“calmness, equanimity”), from aequus (“even; calm; fair”) + animus (“mind, soul”) + -itās. By surface analysis, equ- + anim(us) + -ity.
s: Few people are capable of expressing with equanimity opinions which differ from the prejudices of their social environment.

d: Wrongful conduct by a public official
ety: From Old French malfaisance, derived from malfaire, maufaire (“to do evil”), from Latin malefaciō (“to do evil”), from male (“evilly”) + faciō (“to do, make”).
s: By then, Mr. Altman had gathered more allies. Mr. Nadella, now confident that Mr. Altman was not guilty of malfeasance, threw Microsoft’s weight behind him.

d: One who sets written material into type
ety: From French compositeur, from Latin compositor.
s: I work as an image compositor.

d: Having or showing profound knowledge
ety: From Latin ērudītus, participle of ērudiō (“educate, train”), from e- (“out of”) + rudis (“rude, unskilled”). Doublet of erudit.
s: She was praised for her erudite contributions to the academic journal.

d: A painted or carved screen placed above and behind an altar or communion table
ety: From Middle English reredos, from Anglo-Norman reredos, areredos; equivalent to rere (“rear”) + French dos (“back”).
s: There seem to be no remains of wooden reredoses of the fourteenth century, though there are a number of examples in stone.

d: Having or causing a whirling sensation; liable to falling
ety: From Middle French vertigineux, from Latin vertīginōsus.
s: What began as a drop in support for Israel among younger Democrats has become a vertiginous, across-the-board collapse.

d: Affording an abundant supply
ety: From Middle English plentewos, plentevous, et al., circa 1300, from Old French plentiveus (“fertile, rich”) (early 13th century), from plentif (“abundant”), from plenté (“abundance”) (Modern French pleinté, English plenty), from Latin plenitatem, accusative of plenitas (“fullness”), from plenus (“complete, full”), from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₁nós (“full”).
s: His farm, though small, nevertheless allowed him a plenteous supply of healthy food.

d: Grind and knead
ety: From Latin masticātus, perfect passive participle of masticō (“to chew”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix). Alternatively, back-formation from mastication, either ultimately from Ancient Greek μαστιχάω (mastikháō, “to grind the teeth”). Compare French mastiquer.
s: The cow stood, quietly masticating its cud.

d: A loud harsh or strident noise
ety: From French cacophonie, from Ancient Greek κακοφωνία (kakophōnía), from κακός (kakós, “bad”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound”), equivalent to caco- + -phony.
s: A blistering start from the Scots served to steady the ship amid a cacophony that defied the quarter-full national stadium.

d: Reason with (somebody) for the purpose of dissuasion
ety: From Latin expostulō (“demand, claim”) + -ate (verb-forming suffix). By surface analysis, ex- + postulate.
s: Men expostulate with erring friends; they bring accusations against enemies who have done them a wrong.

d: The part of a ship’s equipment or cargo that is thrown overboard to lighten the load in a storm
ety: From Middle English jetteson, from Anglo-Norman getteson. Doublet of jettison.
s: There she was, floating amongst the jetsam, like so much debris.

d: A scolding (even vicious) old woman
ety: Perhaps a modification of French haridelle (“old horse, nag”).
s: Well there was one old lady, and a drunken old harridan she was surely, that paid all her attention to me.

d: Throw away, of something encumbering
ety: From Anglo-Norman getteson, from Old French getaison, from geter, jeter (modern French: would be *jetaison like pendaison); possibly from a Vulgar Latin *iectātiō, from *iectātus < iectāre, from Latin iactō. Doublet of jetsam.
s: The fuel tanks were jettisoned.

d: Someone who supplies provisions (especially food)
ety: From Middle English purveiour (“one who procures or supplies necessities, provider; city, military, religious, or household employee in charge of provisions, steward; one in charge, overseer; one who goes ahead to prepare the way, forerunner; one who arranges accommodations for a traveller; (figurative) one who gathers greedily”), from Anglo-Norman purveour, Middle French pourveur, pourvoyeur, and
s: The merchants are the purveyors of fine selections.
